0 of 52 drawnGeneral 11Long Meadows 41
The page
  • One beat per panel. Wide strips are 1140×450, catalogue cards 380×450, the attack and approach cards 570×900.
  • The art runs to the exact edge on all four sides: no border, no deckle, no vignette. The game adds the frame.
  • The speech bubble takes the corner named on each panel, about two fifths of its width and height. Keep the subject out of it: the shaded corner on each preview shows where.
  • Nothing that repeats may name an hour: no dusk, dawn or long shadows.
The hand
  • Pen and ink under a thin watercolour wash, on warm off-white paper left bare where it can be.
  • Dust, straw, olive, ochre, stone-grey, faded slate-blue. Nothing lush, nothing neon.
  • Soft, flat, overcast light. Hatching, not solid black, does the shading. Distance goes paler and less drawn.
The world
  • Early medieval, tenth to twelfth century. Timber, wattle, rough stone, thatch. Wool tunics, hoods, leather.
  • No vehicles, glass windows, street lamps or later clothing. Roads are trodden earth with cart ruts.
In a fight
  • The player is on the left facing right, or seen from behind. The opponent faces left, or straight out at the reader.
  • The player: dark brown hair and full beard, plain open helmet, mail to above the knee, leather belt, gloves and high boots, a sword on the right hip and a plain round wooden shield strapped across his back.

General Panels that belong to no biome.

Meeting a threat 2 panels

The two big cards shown when something blocks the road. They are a matched pair at 570x900, and hold the player himself, so draw them as a set.

570×900

ApproachChoice_Avoid

Current art is shown in the preview.

Speech bubble bottom left. So keep the subject high and right.

Choice card, shown beside Engage, and it has to read as the opposite motion to it at a glance. Carries "Slip past them." Going round rather than in. Knees deeply bent and his whole body dropped low, shoulders rolled forward and turned away, one gloved hand out low and open for balance, the other pressing the scabbard flat against his hip to stop it swinging. Weight rolling onto the leading foot with the heel lifted. Head turned to keep something off past the right edge in view while his body carries him past it. Compact and closed where Engage is tall and open: that contrast is the whole read, so make him noticeably lower in the frame than Engage without shrinking him.

Where it sits in the story

After EncIntro_<opponent>, beside ApproachChoice_Engage.

Next DiceRoll for the escape: success shows Avoided_Player then Avoided_<opponent> and the road resumes; failure leads to Challenged and the fight.

570×900

ApproachChoice_Engage

Current art is shown in the preview.

Speech bubble bottom right. So keep the subject high and left.

SIGNATURE RISK: the bubble has the corner the generator wants to sign, so run his body down into the bottom LEFT and sweep the bottom right of the render before accepting it. Choice card, shown beside Avoid, and the widest of the set at 570. Carries "Take them on." Not a blow - the decision to have one. Mid-stride, walking forward toward the right edge: leading boot flat and taking the weight, back leg straight behind him, both shoulders square, head up and level, eyes on something past the right edge. His right hand has crossed to the hilt at his hip and closed on it without drawing. Shield still strapped on his back. Open and upright, the opposite shape to Avoid.

Where it sits in the story

After EncIntro_<opponent>, beside ApproachChoice_Avoid.

Next Challenged, then the player's attack cards.

The Harrowman (the boss of Harrow Field) 2 panels

The wind-up before every attack it makes, and the beat where you slip past it. Draw it the same in both.

The design THE HARROWMAN IS A MAN - a real human fighter. THE SINGLE MOST IMPORTANT FEATURE, and the first thing every prompt says: an iron harrow strapped upright across his back - a flat, ladder-like frame of iron crossbars standing a head and a half above his shoulders, held on by leather straps over both shoulders and across the chest - and EVERY TINE OF IT IS A BLADE. Sickles, billhooks, hand scythes, cleavers and long knives are set into the frame hilt-down, curved edges and points bristling out along it like the teeth of a harrow, so he can draw one over either shoulder without looking. The frame is the silhouette: read it first from any distance. The man himself: tall and gaunt, in his fifties, weathered to the same ash-grey as his field. Close-cropped grey hair, a long hard lined face with a shadowed jaw, pale steady eyes, no expression to speak of - he looks at you the way he looks at a row he has to finish. A long coat of heavy dark sacking-cloth, charred brown at the hem, cinched with a rope belt; grey wool trousers; leather wraps up both forearms; thick gloves; boots caked in ash. Unhurried. He never shouts, never runs, and works in straight lines - advancing, cutting, turning, advancing - the way a plough team works a field. His two weapons, drawn from the frame, are the two attacks. FURROW CUT: a long two-handed pole with a row of short curved blades set along the head of it like the teeth of a rake (the "blade-bar"), driven into the ground and hauled through the soil before it is ripped up. THRESH: a pair of reaping sickles, one in each hand, cutting in fast crossing strokes. Anything else on his back stays in the frame. Say all of that on every panel he appears in; left to itself the generator hands back a knight, or a scarecrow. Nothing on him is straw. No helmet or armour plate, no wheels, no mechanical joints or pistons on the frame - it is plain forged iron and leather.
